# 六维第四个无偏基问题：理论续卷 III

本卷承接[理论续卷 II](MUB_SIX_FOURTH_BASIS_THEORY_CONTINUATION_II.md)，沿用相同的实际输入基约定。第 78 节给出半参数处的完整六十射线分类；第 79 节证明所有非 canonical 正交对的通道均值刚性；第 80 节推出两个半参数附近的 canonical 基唯一性及固定 MUB 对的局部四基排除。区间半径仍为存在性结论。

## 78. Exact sixty-ray census at the half parameter

### 78.1. Statement and complete chart boundary

**Theorem 78.1 (half-parameter census).** At \(b=1/2\), the actual matrix
\(H_0(b)\) has exactly sixty projective common-flat input rays: six canonical
rays, eighteen nonconstant aligned rays, and thirty-six rays whose two
channels each have three distinct entries. The last set consists of all six
synchronous orders above each of six uniquely normalized real quotient
points. This theorem counts rays; orthogonality is treated separately below.

Here a common-flat input ray has a representative \(w\) whose entries have
modulus one and whose image under \(H_0\) also has entries of modulus one.
Theorem 75.1 gives complete coverage on \(0<|b|<1\): canonical zero-mean
modes, the selected three-distinct-channel chart (possibly after \(\Theta\)),
and the aligned finite/pole charts. Theorem 77.1 supplies all eighteen
nonconstant aligned rays at \(b=1/2\), with all its finite rank deficiencies
and the unique-parameter pole case accounted for. We prove the complete
selected-channel count, then show that its thirty-six rays are already
\(\Theta\)-invariant. Thus optional channel selection does not double it.

The certificate below uses rational polynomial identities, exact real-root
isolation, and stated good-prime lifts. It uses no numerical or literature
upper bound. The polynomial data and reconstruction rules needed here are
printed in this section; no unpublished data file is a premise.

### 78.2. Rational channel normalization and original equations

Put \(R=3-b^2\), \(B=3+b^2\), \(h=\sqrt{R/(1+b^2)}\), and
\(\kappa=(b-i)h\). Write the original input as \((x_j,y_j/\kappa)\), so
\(|x_j|^2=1\), \(|y_j|^2=R\), and set \(X=\sum x_j\), \(Y=\sum y_j\).
The original six output equations are equivalent to \(S_j=D_j=0\), where
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_j={}&|X|^2+|Y|^2/R+\Re[(-3+ib)\bar Xx_j-\bar Xy_j
 +\bar Yx_j+(-3-ib)\bar Yy_j/R],\\
D_j={}&\Re[2(b+i)\bar XY+R(b+i)\bar Xx_j+(-2b-iB)\bar Xy_j
 +(-2b+iB)\bar Yx_j-(b-i)\bar Yy_j+2iB\bar x_jy_j].
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{78.1}
\]
Indeed, for the two unnormalized outputs \(A_j,C_j\) of \(\sqrt6H_0\),
\(|A_j|^2+|C_j|^2-12=2S_j\) and
\((1+b^2)h(|A_j|^2-|C_j|^2)=2D_j\) on the input circles. Off those
circles the second formula has additional diagonal term
\(-2bR|x_j|^2+2b|y_j|^2\). Expanding the actual two block rows gives these
identities directly.

In the selected chart fix the unique phase \(X=3t>0\), write
\(x=t\mathbf1+u\), and interpolate
\(y=Gt\mathbf1+Cu+D\bar u\). Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha&=3-ib-\bar G,&\beta&=R+(3+ib)\bar G,\\
Y_c&=\bar GC+G\bar D-|C|^2-|D|^2+C\bar D,\\
L_q&=R(b+i)+(-2b+iB)\bar G,&N&=(-2b-iB)-(b-i)\bar G,\\
T&=3(L_q+NC+\bar N\bar D)-2iB(\bar G+2\bar D-\bar C),\\
E_c&=\bar CT-2iB Y_c,&A_c&=|C|^2+|D|^2,&B_c&=|CD|^2,\\
J_c&=18(b+i)G+3L_q+3NG+2iB(G-C+2D).
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{78.2}
\]
The exact quotient of Theorem 75.3, in these nonsingular scaled coordinates,
is
\[
\begin{gathered}
\beta C+\bar\beta\bar D=-R\alpha,\qquad E_c=0,\\
N_y=(A_c-R)|Y_c|^2+B_c[|G|^2-A_c+4\Re(C\bar D+Y_c)]=0,\\
N_d=\Re(2iBC)|Y_c|^2+B_c\Re J_c+\Re(4iBC|D|^2Y_c)=0.
\end{gathered}                                                    \tag{78.3}
\]
Retain \(\beta CDY_c\ne0\). Put
\[
q=B_c/|Y_c|^2,\quad e=-Y_c/(\bar CD),\quad
\delta=q^2(3-8\Re e)+6q-1.
\tag{78.4}
\]
The strict real domain is \(0<q<1\), \(\delta<0\). Reconstruct
\(t=\sqrt q\), \(\xi=t\bar e\), all six orders of the three distinct unit
roots of \(z^3-3tz^2+3t\xi z-\xi=0\), and the interpolated lower channel,
then divide that channel by \(\kappa\). This is necessary and sufficient,
not only a projected necessary system.

On \(E_c=0\), replace the last two equations by
\[
\begin{aligned}
N_{yD}&=(A_c-R)|T|^2+4B^2|D|^2[|G|^2-A_c+4\Re(C\bar D+Y_c)],\\
N_{dD}&=\Re(2iBC)|T|^2+4B^2|D|^2\Re(J_c+2T).
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{78.5}
\]
Multiplication by \(|C|^2/(4B^2)\) recovers \(N_y,N_d\). The division is
reversible on the retained chart; no zero-denominator stratum is discarded.

### 78.3. Completely specified integer seed construction

Henceforth \(b=1/2\), \(R=11/4\), \(B=13/4\), and
\(G=x+iy\), \(Z=u+iv\), with four real coordinates. Use
\[
C=(Z-R\alpha/2)/\beta,\qquad D=(-\bar Z-R\bar\alpha/2)/\beta.
\tag{78.6}
\]
This parametrizes the linear correlation bijectively. The following rules
fix every scalar and sign used in the certificate tables. For a nonzero
rational polynomial, \(\operatorname{pp}_+\) clears denominators by their
positive least common multiple, divides by the positive gcd of all integer
coefficients, and chooses positive leading coefficient in lexicographic
order \(x,y,u,v\), omitting absent variables. Set
\(\operatorname{pp}_-=-\operatorname{pp}_+\). Complex bars in the construction
fix these real indeterminates and send \(i\) to \(-i\).

Define the following polynomial numerators, before any cancellation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_0&=Z-R\alpha/2,&D_0&=-\bar Z-R\bar\alpha/2,&d&=\beta\bar\beta,\\
A_0&=C_0\bar C_0+D_0\bar D_0,\\
Y_0&=\bar GC_0\bar\beta+G\bar D_0\beta-A_0+C_0\bar D_0,\\
T_0&=3(L_qd+NC_0\bar\beta+\bar N\bar D_0\beta)
       -2iB(\bar Gd+2\bar D_0\beta-\bar C_0\beta),\\
E_0&=\bar C_0T_0-2iB Y_0\bar\beta,\\
J_0&=d\Re[18(b+i)G+3L_q+3NG+2iBG]\\
   &\quad+iB(-C_0\bar\beta+2D_0\bar\beta+\bar C_0\beta-2\bar D_0\beta),\\
W_0&=G\bar Gd-A_0+2(C_0\bar D_0+\bar C_0D_0+Y_0+\bar Y_0),\\
U_Y&=(A_0-Rd)T_0\bar T_0+4B^2D_0\bar D_0dW_0,\\
U_D&=iB(C_0\bar\beta-\bar C_0\beta)T_0\bar T_0
       +4B^2D_0\bar D_0d(J_0+T_0+\bar T_0).
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{78.7}
\]
Set \(E_r=\operatorname{pp}_-(\Re E_0)\),
\(E_i=\operatorname{pp}_-(\Im E_0)\),
\(P_Y=\operatorname{pp}_-(U_Y)\), and
\(P_D=\operatorname{pp}_-(U_D)\). Their leading terms in the stated
lexicographic order are respectively
\(-6512x^4,-244816x^4,-85571732224x^8,-17011456x^8\).
Thus (78.7) specifies the four seed polynomials without storing their large
expanded coefficient lists. All discarded factors are nonzero rational
scalars or powers of \(\beta\bar\beta\).

Write \(E_r=au+b_0v+c_0\), and put
\[
\beta_0=148x^2+264x+148y^2+44y+121=16|\beta|^2.
\tag{78.8}
\]
For a polynomial \(P=\sum_{j=0}^m p_j u^j\), define its full cleared
substitution \(\mathcal S(P)=\sum_jp_j(-b_0v-c_0)^ja^{m-j}\), where
\(m=\deg_uP\). Define
\[
Q=\operatorname{pp}_-\mathcal S(E_i),\quad
Y=\operatorname{pp}_+\mathcal S(P_Y),\quad
D=\operatorname{pp}_+\mathcal S(P_D).
\tag{78.9}
\]
These have \(v\)-degrees \(2,4,3\); no factor independent of \(v\) is
removed. Write \(Q=q_2v^2+Lv+K\), set
\(F_8=\operatorname{pp}_+(q_2)\), and verify \(q_2=3328F_8\).

For the exceptional linear stratum, first reduce every coefficient of
\(Q,Y,D\) modulo \(F_8\) by ordinary division in \(x\) over \(\mathbb Q[y]\),
and primitive-normalize each whole result with positive leading coefficient.
Call them \(Q_0=L_0v+K_0,Y_0',D_0'\). For \(P=\sum p_jv^j\) of degree
\(m\), put \(\mathcal T(P)=\sum_jp_j(-K_0)^jL_0^{m-j}\). Define
\[
H_Y=\operatorname{pp}_+\operatorname{rem}_x(\mathcal T(Y_0'),F_8),\quad
H_D=\operatorname{pp}_+\operatorname{rem}_x(\mathcal T(D_0'),F_8).
\tag{78.10}
\]
Their total degrees are 30 and 23. The reduced \(L_0,K_0\) differ from the
reductions of \(L,K\) only by the same nonzero rational scalar.

### 78.4. Exhausting every exceptional stratum

The finite rational traces in §78.B establish the following identities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1&\in(a,E_r,E_i,P_Y,P_D,w\beta_0-1),\\
(a\beta_0 f_4)^2&\in(F_8,L,K),\\
(a\beta_0 L)^3&\in(F_8,H_Y,H_D),
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{78.11}
\]
where
\[
f_4=3382096y^4+12165296y^3+23734128y^2+33454564y+40319015.
\]
Its signed primitive Sturm chain has no real root.
The first identity excludes \(a=0\) when \(\beta_0\ne0\).
For \(a\ne0,F_8=0\), if \(L=0\), the equation \(Q=0\) also forces \(K=0\),
and the second identity is impossible over the reals. If \(L\ne0\), then
\(v=-K/L\); the divided norms force \(H_Y=H_D=0\), contradicting the third
identity. Thus every physical point lies on \(a\beta_0F_8\ne0\). This split
retains both the substitution pole and every degree-drop case of \(Q\).

### 78.5. Regular projection, exact resultant, and component exclusions

Let \(\operatorname{prem}_v\) be pseudo-remainder with the conventional
multiplier \(\operatorname{lc}(Q)^{\deg P-\deg Q+1}\). Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_Yv+B_Y&=\operatorname{pp}_-
 \left(\frac{\operatorname{prem}_v(Y,Q)}{\beta_0^2a^3F_8^2}\right),\\
A_Dv+B_D&=\operatorname{pp}_+
 \left(\frac{\operatorname{prem}_v(D,Q)}{\beta_0^2a^2F_8}\right),\\
F_{16}&=\operatorname{pp}_+
 \left(\frac{A_YB_D-B_YA_D}{\beta_0aF_8}\right),\\
R_Y&=\operatorname{rem}_x(KA_Y^2-LA_YB_Y+q_2B_Y^2,F_{16}),\\
R_D&=\operatorname{pp}_+\operatorname{rem}_x(KA_D^2-LA_DB_D+q_2B_D^2,F_{16}).
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{78.12}
\]
All three indicated divisions are exact up to the retained nonzero rational
constants; the quotient polynomials have respectively total degrees
15,15,16. The \(x\)-leading coefficient of \(F_{16}\) is the nonzero constant
38238657380352. Both \(F_{16}=R_Y=0\) are necessary, even if
\(A_Y=B_Y=0\); no division by either linear coefficient has been made.

Here are deterministic rules for the exact projection certificate. Start
\(V_0=F_{16}\), \(V_1=\operatorname{pp}_+(R_Y)\). For successive pairs
\(A,B\), compute \(P=\operatorname{prem}_x(A,B)\). Let \(c\) be the gcd over
\(\mathbb Z[y]\) of its coefficients in \(x\), including their integer
content, chosen with positive leading coefficient in \(y\). Append
\(P/c\), retaining its sign, and record \(c\). The degrees in \(x\) are
16,15,14,...,1,0; the last polynomial is 1. At each of the first fourteen
steps, \(c\) is a nonzero rational multiple of \(\operatorname{lc}_x(A)^2\).
These are exact rational polynomial division identities.

For degrees \(n+1,n,n-1\), the resultant recurrence is
\[
\operatorname{Res}(A,B)=c^n\operatorname{lc}_x(B)^{2-2n}
 \operatorname{Res}(B,P/c).
\tag{78.13}
\]
(The sign \((-1)^{n(n+1)}\) is 1.) Consequently the primitive resultant is
\(\operatorname{pp}_+(c_{14}/\operatorname{lc}_x(V_{14})^2)\), where
\(V_{14}\) has degree two. It has degree 304. This is a polynomial
resultant identity, so necessity does not assume that intermediate leading
coefficients remain nonzero after specialization.

Its exact primitive factorization is the product of the polynomials in
§78.A with the multiplicities in their labels. Their real-root counts are:

| Multiplicity | Factor degrees, in printed order | Real-root counts |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4,8,20,52 | 0,0,8,8 |
| 2 | 2,4,4,14,30,50 | 0,0,0,0,10,10 |
| 3 | 4 | 0 |

Each count follows by the signed primitive Sturm sequence over the integers.
Thus only factors of degrees 20,30,50,52 need be considered. On each, all
fourteen nonterminal contents, the \(x\)-coefficient of \(V_{15}\), and the
factor derivative are units. The next table gives their sixteen nonzero
multiplication-norm residues, in that order. Reduction retains the full
factor degree and every rational denominator.

| Degree | Prime | Sixteen residues |
|---|---|---|
|20|97|6,75,72,70,75,2,6,85,32,75,72,47,94,73,35,40|
|52|107|23,87,62,40,23,4,48,47,86,25,49,92,102,86,53,104|
|30|101|14,88,68,100,25,49,96,79,78,58,56,13,43,85,45,63|
|50|97|93,66,66,73,9,8,61,88,91,50,4,27,54,93,12,65|

For each real candidate factor \(f\), reduce \(V_{15}=A(y)x+B(y)\) modulo
\(f\) and set \(x=-B/A\) in \(\mathbb Q[y]/(f)\). This uniquely determines
its possible \(x\). For a short exact replay, §78.A also prints the three
numerators \(P_{\mathrm{proj},d}\), \(d=52,30,50\): substitution shows
\(x=P_{\mathrm{proj},d}/f'\) satisfies \(V_{15}=0\). The certified units
make these expressions the same unique solution. Exact homogeneous
substitution and polynomial division give \(F_8=0\) on degree 52 and
\(a=0\) on degree 30, both excluded above. On degree 50 they give
\(A_Y=B_Y=0\), while \(A_D\) and \(R_D\) are units: their multiplication
norms modulo 97 are 12 and 17. Thus the second compatibility is impossible.
These exclusions do not require irreducibility or numerical approximations.

### 78.6. Exact real quotient and projective counting

Let \(f=f_{1,20}\) in §78.A. The three printed numerator lists define
\[
(x,u,v)=(P_x,P_u,P_v)/f'(y).                              \tag{78.14}
\]
Exact homogeneous substitution and integer polynomial division show that
(78.14) satisfies \(V_{15}=0\) and all four original numerator equations
\(E_r,E_i,P_Y,P_D=0\). The elements \(\beta_0,a,F_8,A_Y\) are units in
\(\mathbb Q[y]/(f)\): their norms modulo 97 are 7,36,26,17. Consequently
\(v=-B_Y/A_Y\) and \(u=-(b_0v+c_0)/a\) are unique. Thus this RUR describes
every remaining possible physical quotient point, in both directions.

The eight rational intervals in §78.C each contain one simple root of
\(f\), and the complete Sturm count is eight. Evaluate (78.14), then
(78.6),(78.2),(78.4), by rational interval arithmetic: Horner evaluation
for each coefficient list and its derivative, complex division via the
positive squared modulus, and outward rounding after each real operation
to multiples of \(2^{-512}\). The printed coarse enclosures are verified
strict inclusions. In every interval \(\beta,C,D,Y_c\) have positive lower
bounds for their squared moduli. Roots 0,1,2,5,6,7 satisfy the strict domain;
root 3 has \(q>1\), and root 4 has \(\delta>0\). Hence there are exactly six
physical selected-channel quotient points.

For these six, the same enclosures give \(|C|^2-|D|^2\ne0\). Equal lower
entries corresponding to two distinct upper roots would imply
\((z_i-z_j)(C-D/(z_i z_j))=0\), and therefore \(|C|=|D|\), a contradiction.
Both channels are three-distinct. Their means are nonzero by Theorem 75.2,
so \(\Theta\) maps all thirty-six rays back into the selected chart. The
complete classification makes this set \(\Theta\)-invariant.

The six orders at each quotient point are distinct because the phase
\(X=3t>0\) is unique and the three upper roots are distinct. Different
quotient points cannot coincide projectively: means and interpolation
recover \(G,C,D\), hence \(Z\), uniquely. These thirty-six rays are disjoint
from the aligned set and the canonical zero-mean modes; the two constant
canonical rays were separated from the eighteen nonconstant aligned rays
in §77. The disjoint count is \(36+18+6=60\), proving Theorem 78.1.

### 78.B. Finite rational ideal-membership traces
The three tables below are executable polynomial identities. In the stated grevlex variable order, let row `S k` be seed k; `R j [d1,...,dn]` is the monic nonzero remainder of row j under ordinary ordered multivariate division by the listed earlier rows. Empty divisor lists are allowed. A row `M j e k f` means monomial `e` times row j minus monomial `f` times row k; exponent vectors use the stated variable order. Every scalar in these M rows is exactly +1 or −1. Rows are numbered from zero; no inferred Gröbner-completeness assertion is used. Each division strictly descends in leading monomial. Therefore every reconstructed row lies in the seed ideal. The terminal assertions printed after the tables complete the ideal-membership certificates.

```text
177: R 166 168,170,172
178: R 168 170,172
179: R 170 172
```
Terminal identity: start r₀=1 and repeat rⱼ₊₁=rem((aβ₀L)rⱼ; rows 173,174,175,176,177,178,179,172,6) for 3 steps. The final remainder is zero. Thus (aβ₀L)^3 belongs to the seed ideal.

## 79. Complete noncanonical pair rigidity at the half parameter

### 79.1. Statement and exact coefficient algebra

**Theorem 79.1 (all-pair mean-spinor rigidity).** At \(b=1/2\), every
orthogonal pair of noncanonical common-flat input rays has orthogonal
nonzero channel-mean spinors. There are no generic–aligned orthogonal
pairs. In particular, there is no orthogonal triple of noncanonical rays.

Theorem 78.1 partitions the noncanonical set into the full thirty-six-ray
generic set and eighteen-ray aligned set. Both contain their optional
\(\Theta\) images. The following calculations retain all relative root
orders. Synchronous covariance is used to compress certificates, not to
restrict candidate pairs. The aligned–aligned implication is Theorem 77.1.

Rename the real quotient variable of §78 as \(\eta\), and set
\[
\mathcal A=\mathbb Q(i)[\eta]/(f_{1,20}(\eta)),\qquad
(x,u,v)=(P_x,P_u,P_v)/f_{1,20}'(\eta).
\tag{79.1}
\]
Use \(G=x+i\eta,Z=u+iv\) and the expressions of (78.2),(78.4),(78.6).
A bar fixes \(\eta\) and rational coefficients and sends \(i\) to \(-i\).
All original undivided quotient equations hold in this algebra. It is
reduced. Put
\[
\Delta=D\bar D-C\bar C,\qquad
\delta=q^2[3-4(e+\bar e)]+6q-1.
\]
The following multiplication norms modulo 97, with \(i\mapsto22\), are
nonzero. They fix all inverse and separability hypotheses below.

| Element | Norm | Element | Norm |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| \(f'/\operatorname{lc}(f)\) |87| \(G\) |92|
| \(\bar G\) |82| \(\beta\) |89|
| \(\bar\beta\) |80| \(C\) |25|
| \(\bar C\) |64| \(D\) |80|
| \(\bar D\) |46| \(Y_c\) |39|
| \(\bar Y_c\) |55| \(q\) |62|
| \(q-1\) |92| \(e\) |12|
| \(\bar e\) |3| \(\delta\) |53|
| \(\Delta\) |75| \(qG\bar G/R\) |62|
| \(qG\bar G/R-1\) |92| | |

These residues are reconstructible by multiplication matrices in the basis
\(1,\eta,\ldots,\eta^{19}\), using the printed coefficient lists of §78.A.
The full degree and all scalar denominators have good reduction. Every
inverse used to construct an element is checked first in the same quotient.
Thus a nonzero norm proves a unit in characteristic zero; it is not a
modular-only assertion about the physical solution set.

For a physical quotient point the original channel-mean spinor is
proportional to \((1,G/\kappa)\). Its pairing with a second point vanishes
exactly when
\[
M=1+\bar GG'/R=0.                                       \tag{79.2}
\]

### 79.2. Exact antiunitary transport on all twenty algebra points

The following substitution defines an involutive automorphism \(\sigma\)
of \(\mathcal A\):
\[
x_\sigma=-Rx/(x^2+\eta^2),\qquad
\eta_\sigma=-R\eta/(x^2+\eta^2).
\tag{79.3}
\]
Indeed, substitute (79.3) homogeneously into the printed polynomials:
\(f(\eta_\sigma)=0\), and
\(P_x(\eta_\sigma)/f'(\eta_\sigma)=x_\sigma\), as exact polynomial
remainders modulo \(f\). The denominator \(G\bar G\) is a unit. The
substitution squares to the identity, so it is an automorphism. The same
rational substitution, clearing denominators and reducing real and
imaginary integer coefficients separately modulo \(f\), gives
\[
G_\sigma=-R/\bar G,\quad
C_\sigma=RC/\Delta,\quad
D_\sigma=-RG\bar D/(\bar G\Delta),\quad
q_\sigma=qG\bar G/R.                                    \tag{79.4}
\]
These are identities on the entire degree-twenty algebra, not evaluations
at its six physical points. A compact additional identity for the last
formula is
\[
U=(D-C)\Delta-G(C\bar C+D\bar D)-\bar GCD,
\qquad U\bar U=RY_c\bar Y_c.
\tag{79.5}
\]
It follows by the same cleared integer remainder calculation and gives the
last equality of (79.4) after substituting the first three.

The geometric interpretation fixes the normalization. In the scaled
coordinates the projective antiunitary is
\(J_R(x,y)=(-\bar y/\sqrt R,\sqrt R\bar x)\), differing from the original
\(\Theta\) by one common unit phase. For
\(x=t\mathbf1+u,y=Gt\mathbf1+Cu+D\bar u\), choose \(t_\sigma^2=q_\sigma\).
Normalizing the first channel mean to \(3t_\sigma\) gives
\[
x_\sigma=t_\sigma[\mathbf1+(\bar Du+\bar C\bar u)/(\bar Gt)],\qquad
y_\sigma=-Rt_\sigma(\mathbf1+\bar u/t)/\bar G.
\tag{79.6}
\]
The centered change of basis is invertible because \(\Delta\) is a unit.
Its two-by-two interpolation gives (79.4), and the phase multiplier has
squared norm \(Rq_\sigma/(qG\bar G)=1\).

The argument also holds in a faithful finite splitting algebra: adjoin
\(t^2=q\), fixed by bar, and all roots of the reciprocal cubic of §78.2.
The circle identities are algebraic, with bar sending a root to its inverse;
all stated denominators and the cubic discriminant are units. The invertible
centered change preserves the three-distinct interpolation. Its correlation
and product identities recover the transformed cubic as well. Hence the
\(\sigma\)-point represents \(J_Rw\), up to phase and one of the six orders,
in this splitting algebra. No real inequality is imposed on non-real
coefficient points.

### 79.3. Reconstructible six-order norm

Write \(E=\bar e\). The normalized upper roots \(Z_j=x_j/t\) satisfy
\[
f_Z(Z)=Z^3-3Z^2+3EZ-E/q,\quad
\mathcal B(Z)=(Z^2-3Z+3E)/E=\bar Z,\quad
\mathcal L(Z)=G+C(Z-1)+D(\mathcal B(Z)-1).
\tag{79.7}
\]
The cubic discriminant is \(27E^2\delta/q^2\), a unit.
Here is a finite coefficient construction of the product of all six
relative ordinary overlaps, divided by \((3tt')^6\).
Write ordered triples as \(1+a\omega^j+b\omega^{-j}\) and
\(1+c\omega^j+d\omega^{-j}\), and put
\[
\begin{aligned}
P&=ab=1-E,&S&=a^3+b^3=2-3E+E/q,\\
Q&=cd=1-E',&T&=c^3+d^3=2-3E'+E'/q',\\
H&=\bar C/E,&K&=\bar D-H,&F&=C'-D'/E',&J&=D'/E',\\
A_0&=1/E+HF/R,&B_0&=-1/E+KF/R,&C_0&=HJ/R,&D_0&=KJ/R,\\
m&=1+\bar GG'/R,\\
L_0&=A_0a^2c+B_0bc+C_0a^2d^2+D_0bd^2,\\
L_1&=A_0b^2d+B_0ad+C_0b^2c^2+D_0ac^2.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{79.8}
\]
Expand
\[
\mathcal F=(m^3+L_0^3+L_1^3-3mL_0L_1)
 (m^3+L_0^3+L_1^3-3mL_0L_1)_{c\leftrightarrow d}.
\tag{79.9}
\]
It is separately symmetric in \(a,b\) and \(c,d\). In every monomial the
exponent difference within each pair is divisible by three. The following
explicit rule eliminates these four indeterminates without any root choices.
Group monomials into their orbits under the two exchanges. For one pair,
replace the orbit sum of \(a^rb^s\) by \(P^r\) if \(r=s\), and otherwise by
\(P^{\min(r,s)}U_{|r-s|/3}\), where
\(U_0=2,U_1=S,U_n=SU_{n-1}-P^3U_{n-2}\). Use the same rule with \(Q,T\)
for the second pair. Multiply the two orbit sums and their common original
coefficient. This gives an integer polynomial
\(\mathcal N(A_0,B_0,C_0,D_0,m,P,S,Q,T)\), with 508 nonzero terms.
Equation (79.9) is its exact pullback identity and specifies every coefficient.

Evaluate these nine arguments in \(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\), with
primes denoting the second factor, and call the resulting element \(N\).
The three cyclic overlaps divided by \(3tt'\) are
\(m+\omega^kL_0+\omega^{-k}L_1\); their product is the first factor in
(79.9). Exchanging \(c,d\) gives the other three orders. Therefore an
orthogonal generic pair always annihilates \(N\).

### 79.4. Matching characteristic-zero upper rank and exact lower minor

Define the surjection
\[
\rho:\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\longrightarrow\mathcal A,
\qquad \rho(a\otimes b)=a\sigma(b).
\]
Its kernel has dimension \(400-20=380\). At the \(\sigma\)-point one of the
six relative rays is \(J_Rw\), by §79.2, and its overlap vanishes identically:
\[
\sum_j[\bar x_j(-\bar y_j/\sqrt R)
       +\bar y_j(\sqrt R\bar x_j)/R]=0.
\]
In the faithful splitting algebra one factor of (79.9) therefore vanishes.
Faithfulness gives \(\rho(N)=0\) in characteristic zero. Consequently the
image of multiplication by \(N\) lies in \(\ker\rho\) and has dimension
at most 380. This is an all-algebra-point identity, not a sampled-real-root
rank bound.

For the lower bound, reconstruct \(N\) by (79.8)–(79.9) from §78.A, reduce
modulo 97 with \(i=22\), and form its multiplication matrix in the ordered
basis \(\eta^r\otimes\eta^s\), \(0\le r,s<20\), indexed by \(20r+s\).
The leading \(380\times380\) principal minor has determinant
\[
2\pmod {97}.                                             \tag{79.10}
\]
This is a complete reconstruction rule for the minor: each column is
\(N\eta^r\otimes\eta^s\), reduced separately by the monic degree-twenty
factor in each variable; retain row and column indices 0 through 379.
All reductions and inverses have good reduction by §79.1. Thus (79.10)
proves characteristic-zero rank at least 380. Together the two bounds give
\[
N(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A)=\ker\rho.                  \tag{79.11}
\]
Moreover \(\rho(M)=1+\bar G(-R/\bar G)/R=0\), so \(M\in(N)\). Evaluation
at a physical orthogonal pair annihilates \(N\), hence also \(M\). This
proves the required generic–generic mean-spinor implication in every order.

### 79.5. Mixed pairs and a full multiplication determinant

Use the exact degree-five aligned algebra of §77. Write its quintic variable
as \(d\), set \(s^2=K(d)=d^2+4\tau(d)\), where \(\tau\) is (77.5),
and take \(a(d)=A(d,\tau(d))\), \(c(d)=C_a(d,\tau(d))\) from the
first-two-row Cramer solutions in §77.2, using the original system (75.26). The scaled aligned representative is
\[
(1,1,z;H,H,Hr),\quad
z=\frac{2+i(s+d)}{2-i(s+d)},\quad
r=\frac{2+i(s-d)}{2-i(s-d)},\quad H=s(a+ic).
\tag{79.12}
\]
Here \(H\) is the scaled lower phase \(\kappa g\), of squared modulus \(R\),
not the original unit phase \(g\). Both signs of \(s\), all three physical
quintic roots, and all three unique-position choices are retained. The
finite/pole exclusions are already part of Theorem 77.1.

For a generic normalized root \(Z\) at the unique aligned position, the
ordinary overlap divided by \(t\) is \(A_mZ^2+B_mZ+C_m\), where
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_m&=(z-1)/E+(H/R)(r-1)\bar C/E,\\
B_m&=-3(z-1)/E+(H/R)(r-1)(\bar D-3\bar C/E),\\
C_m&=3z+3\bar GH/R+(H/R)(r-1)(\bar G+2\bar C-\bar D).
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{79.13}
\]
This follows by summing the two repeated positions in the original overlap.
Let
\[
C_Z=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&E/q\\1&0&-3E\\0&1&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
N_m=\det(A_mC_Z^2+B_mC_Z+C_mI_3).
\tag{79.14}
\]
It is the product over the three possible relative unique positions.
In
\[
\mathcal A\otimes\mathbb Q(i)[d,s]/(f_5(d),s^2-K(d)),
\]
the full multiplication determinant of \(N_m\) equals
\[
57\pmod {97},\qquad i\mapsto22.                          \tag{79.15}
\]
To reconstruct it, use basis \(s^\epsilon\eta^rd^j\), indexed by
\(100\epsilon+5r+j\), with \(\epsilon=0,1\), \(0\le r<20\), \(0\le j<5\).
Reduce each column by the two monic factors and \(s^2=K(d)\). The aligned
coordinate functions, quintic, and inverses are exactly those in (77.1)–
(77.6); all scalar and polynomial denominators, including those in (79.12),
are checked invertible modulo 97 and the factor degrees remain 20 and 5.
More explicitly, the aligned norms of \(K,J,F_0,(2-22d)^2+K,
(2+22d)^2+K\) are respectively \(51,37,90,15,36\), where
\(J=d-2\tau(d)+6\), \(F_0=d^2+(\tau(d)+1)^2\).
Thus (79.15) lifts to invertibility in characteristic zero. No mixed physical
pair can annihilate \(N_m\), so there is no generic–aligned orthogonal edge.

Generic pairs now satisfy (79.2), mixed edges are absent, and aligned pairs
satisfy the same mean-spinor implication by Theorem 77.1. The channel means
are nonzero by Theorem 75.2. An orthogonal noncanonical triple would give
three mutually orthogonal nonzero vectors in \(\mathbb C^2\), impossible.
This proves Theorem 79.1.


## 80. Canonical-basis uniqueness near both half parameters

**Theorem 80.1 (two open parameter neighborhoods).** At \(b=\pm1/2\),
the only common-flat orthonormal input basis is the canonical basis, up to
column phases and permutation. There exists \(\varepsilon>0\), which may
be chosen less than \(1/4\), such that the same uniqueness holds whenever
\[
|b-1/2|<\varepsilon\quad\text{or}\quad|b+1/2|<\varepsilon.
\tag{80.1}
\]
For every such \(b\), the fixed mutually-unbiased pair \((I_6,H_0(b))\)
cannot be part of a quartet. The radius here is existential.

At \(b=1/2\), a common-flat orthonormal basis containing a canonical ray is
entirely canonical by Proposition 60.1. A basis containing none would contain
an orthogonal noncanonical triple, contrary to Theorem 79.1. This proves the
positive pointwise statement without presupposing intersection with the
canonical set.

The negative parameter is transported by the exact identity
\[
H_0(-b)=\operatorname{diag}(I_3,-I_3)\,H_0(b)
 \begin{pmatrix}0&I_3\\I_3&0\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{80.2}
\]
These monomial factors preserve flatness and orthogonality. Swapping input
channels also maps the canonical ray set onto its negative-parameter set,
so the same pointwise statement holds at \(-1/2\).

For the neighborhood assertion, take \(K=[1/4,3/4]\). Corollary 62.2 gives
\(\eta_K>0\) separating every noncanonical common-flat orthonormal input
basis at \(b\in K\) from the moving canonical basis modulo phases and
permutations. If uniqueness failed arbitrarily close to \(1/2\), choose
\(b_n\to1/2\) and such noncanonical unitary bases \(W_n\). Compactness of
\(U(6)\) gives a convergent subsequence. Orthonormality and original
input/output flatness are closed conditions, so its limit \(W_*\) is a
common-flat basis at \(1/2\). Pointwise uniqueness makes it canonical up
to a fixed column phase/permutation choice. The full Gram matrix remains
the identity in the limit; distinct orthogonal columns cannot collide.
Continuity of the canonical matrix \(C(b)\) then makes the distance from
\(W_n\) to the moving canonical class tend to zero, contradicting
\(\eta_K\). This gives an open interval. Equation (80.2) gives its negative
counterpart; shrink the common radius below \(1/4\).

Finally keep the input/output convention explicit. A unitary column basis
\(B\) is unbiased to both \(I_6\) and \(H_0(b)\) exactly when
\(W=H_0(b)^*B\) is unitary and both \(W\) and \(H_0(b)W=B\) are flat.
Thus the unique ordinary common-unbiased basis is
\(H_0(b)C(b)/\sqrt6\), up to column phases and permutation, where \(C(b)\)
is the unit-entry canonical **input** matrix of (62.1). Two additional bases
in a quartet would have that same column-ray set. Their relative unitary
would be monomial, which cannot be flat. This proves the fixed-pair
no-quartet corollary on (80.1).

No numerical radius is asserted, and these intervals have not been shown
to join the central neighborhood of §§67–69. The entire nonzero open branch
and the general dimension-six fourth-MUB problem remain outside this result.
